Security ticket for the session service (CWE-347). Problem: `decode` only checks the signature when the token has one: `header.payload.` (an empty signature part) is accepted as if it were signed, so anyone can mint a token such as `{"sub": "admin"}` without knowing the secret. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

A penetration test of the partner API reported a vulnerability: `decode` lets the token's own header choose the algorithm: `{"alg": "none"}` skips the signature check completely, so a token with any claims and no signature is accepted (the classic `alg=none` JWT bypass); other `alg` values are quietly treated as HS256. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Review comment on `decode`: `decode` verifies the signature but never looks at `exp` or `nbf`, so a token that expired last year (or was stolen from an old backup) is accepted forever, and tokens cannot be revoked by letting them time out. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

A penetration test of the token service with rotating keys reported a vulnerability: `decode` joins the unchecked `kid` header onto the key directory and reads that file as the HMAC key: `kid: "../public/robots.txt"` (or an absolute path, or `/dev/null`) makes the key a file whose content the attacker knows, so any token can be forged and arbitrary readable files are opened. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Our static analysis flagged `decode` (CWE-345): `decode` checks the signature only: the services share one signing secret, so a valid token issued by the *login* service for the *search* service (or for another tenant's issuer) is accepted by the billing API as well; a token meant for a low-privilege audience can be replayed against a high-privilege one. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

We had an incident review for the API gateway. Root cause: `verify` picks the verification method from the token's `alg` header and keeps a legacy `HS256` branch that uses the gateway's *public key* as the HMAC secret; the public key is public, so an attacker signs `{"role": "admin"}` with HS256 using that key text and the gateway accepts it (key/algorithm confusion). Close the hole in `verify` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

log_login_failure is unsafe: `log_login_failure` writes the submitted user name into the log line as typed: a user name like `admin from 10.0.0.5\nINFO login succeeded for user admin from 10.0.0.5` forges a second log entry that the security team (and the log-based alerting) will believe. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Review comment on `handle_login`: `handle_login` logs the whole submitted form with `logger.info("login attempt: %s", form)`: every password (and CSRF token, and mistyped password of a real user) lands in the application log, the log shipper and the support team's search tool. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

A penetration test of the structured logger reported a vulnerability: `log_event` builds the JSON line with string formatting: a message such as `x", "level": "debug` (or one containing a newline, a backslash or a quote) changes the fields of the record, injects whole fake entries, or produces invalid JSON that the log pipeline drops - including the entries around it. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the audit trail. Root cause: `format_event` joins `key=value` pairs without quoting: an action such as `delete user=admin role=root` (typed into a free-text field) adds fields to the entry, a value with a newline writes a second, forged entry, and values with spaces make the line impossible to parse reliably. Close the hole in `format_event` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Review comment on `describe_request`: `describe_request` writes the request path and user agent unbounded and unescaped: one request with a 5 MB path fills the log disk (and every downstream indexer), and control characters in the user agent split lines or paint terminal escape sequences into an admin's `tail -f`. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `update_profile` (CWE-915): `update_profile` copies every submitted form field into the profile, so a request with an extra `is_admin=true`, `verified=true` or `id=1` field (the edit form has no such inputs, but nothing stops a client from sending them) escalates privileges: mass assignment. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `create_order` (CWE-915): `create_order` takes the unit price from the cart item when the client supplies one, so `{"sku": "backpack", "qty": 1, "price": 1}` buys a backpack for one cent (the price is a server-side fact, not user input), and quantities are not validated (negative quantities give refunds). Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

A penetration test of the account service reported a vulnerability: `Account.__init__` and `update` run `setattr` for every key the caller passes, and the keys come straight from the request body: `{"is_admin": true, "credits": 100000}` creates a privileged account, and keys such as `save` or `__class__` replace methods or break the object. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Security ticket for the user import (CWE-915). Problem: `import_users` applies the `role` and `disabled` columns of an uploaded file no matter who uploads it, so any user allowed to import a roster of colleagues can add themselves as an admin (and re-enable disabled accounts) through two extra columns. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

A penetration test of the settings API reported a vulnerability: `apply_patch` deep-merges whatever JSON the client sends: a patch like `{"billing": {"plan": "enterprise", "seats": 9999}}` upgrades the account for free, `{"limits": {"max_items": 10**9}}` removes the quota, and wrongly typed values end up in the settings. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Review comment on `after_login`: `after_login` redirects to whatever `next` contains, so a phishing mail with `/login?next=https://evil.io/fake-dashboard` sends users to an attacker's site right after they typed their real password. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

A penetration test of the identity provider reported a vulnerability: `validate_redirect_uri` accepts any URI that merely *starts with* a registered one, so `https://app.example.net/oauth/callback/../../evil` and `https://app.example.net/oauth/callback?next=https://evil.io` pass, and an authorization code can be delivered to a page the client never registered (open redirect, account takeover). Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Security ticket for the logout and consent screens (CWE-601). Problem: `safe_return_to` accepts anything that starts with `/` or merely *contains* the site's host name, so `//evil.io`, `https://app.example.com.evil.io/`, `https://evil.io/?app.example.com` and `https://app.example.com@evil.io/` all redirect off-site. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

We had an incident review for the documentation server. Root cause: `slash_redirect` echoes the request path into `Location`; a request for `//evil.io` (or `/\evil.io`) is answered with `Location: //evil.io/`, which browsers read as a link to another site, so any link to the docs server can be turned into a redirector. Close the hole in `slash_redirect` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Our static analysis flagged `safe_redirect` (CWE-601): `safe_redirect` only checks that `urlparse` finds no network location, which `/\evil.io`, `\\evil.io`, `https:evil.io`, `javascript:alert(1)` and a tab in `/	/evil.io` all satisfy, although browsers read each of them as a link to another site (or to script). Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Security ticket for the customer portal (CWE-601). Problem: `login_target` screens the value of `next` for `http`, `//` and `://` and decodes it afterwards: `next=%252F%252Fevil.io` (or `/%252Fevil.io`) passes the screening and becomes `//evil.io` after the second decoding, an open redirect. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Review comment on `UserStore.register`: `register` stores the password itself in `users`: every database dump, backup or debug log of that table hands out working credentials (which users reuse elsewhere). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Security ticket for the sign-up form (CWE-521). Problem: `validate_password` only requires 8 characters: `password1`, `12345678` and the user's own name pass, there is no upper bound (a 10 MB password is a cheap denial of service against the hash function) and common passwords are not rejected, so accounts are trivially guessable. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

We had an incident review for the shop login. Root cause: Login answers `404 no such user` for unknown names and `401 wrong password` for known ones, and the reset form answers differently for registered and unknown addresses, so anyone can test which users and e-mail addresses have accounts (account enumeration), the first step of credential stuffing and targeted phishing. Close the hole in `Accounts.login` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

We had an incident review for the customer portal. Root cause: `hash_password` and `verify_password` cut the password to its first 8 characters (a leftover from the old crypt(3) limit), so `correct horse battery staple` and `correct ` are the same password: long passphrases protect nothing beyond 8 characters and anyone who guesses the prefix gets in. Close the hole in `hash_password` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

A penetration test of the intranet reported a vulnerability: `hash_password` is a bare, unsalted MD5: a leaked table is cracked at billions of guesses per second with rainbow tables, and equal passwords are visible as equal hashes. The existing users' records are MD5 hex strings, so the fix must migrate without locking them out. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

ResetService.issue is unsafe: `issue` stores the reset token itself as the primary key of the `rows` table: anyone who can read the table (a SQL injection, a backup, a replica) can open every pending reset link and take over those accounts without touching a password. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Security ticket for the profile service (CWE-22). Problem: `load_avatar` opens `os.path.join(AVATAR_DIR, name)` for whatever `name` the request supplies, so a name like `../secret.txt` (or an absolute path) reads files outside the avatar directory. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

read_note is unsafe: `read_note` strips `../` from the note name before opening it, but `....//secret` turns into `../secret` after the replacement, and the sanitising does not stop absolute paths either. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

A penetration test of the reporting service reported a vulnerability: `open_report` checks that the resolved path starts with the reports directory, but a sibling directory such as `reports_private` shares that prefix, so `../reports_private/q3.csv` passes the check. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

serve_static is unsafe: `serve_static` rejects paths with a `..` segment but only looks at the raw request path and percent-decodes it afterwards, so `/%2e%2e/secret.txt`, `/..%2fsecret.txt` and an encoded absolute path all get through. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Our static analysis flagged `render` (CWE-22): template names, including the names in `{% include ... %}` tags that anyone with template-edit rights can write, are joined to the template directory without checking, so `{% include ../../secret %}` pulls in files from elsewhere. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Security ticket for the ticket system (CWE-59). Problem: `read_attachment` compares absolute paths lexically, but attachments are unpacked from customer archives and can contain symbolic links, so a link inside a ticket folder that points to `../../secret.txt` is followed when the file is opened. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Our static analysis flagged `tail_log` (CWE-22): `tail_log` rejects any name containing `..`, which still lets an absolute path like `/var/secret/app.key` through (`os.path.join` drops the log directory), and the substring test also wrongly rejects legitimate files such as `build..old.log`. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

serve is unsafe: the handlers normalise the request path with `os.path.normpath('/' + path)` and then `os.path.join` it to the site directory - an absolute path in the request replaces the site directory entirely, so `serve`, `list_dir` and `exists` all work on any file on the machine (and `exists` is a file-existence oracle). fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

We had an incident review for the backup tool. Root cause: `restore(backup_name, target_name)` joins both names to their directories without checking: a target such as `../config.ini` overwrites files outside the data directory (and creates directories there), and a backup name such as `../secret.txt` copies arbitrary files into the data directory. Close the hole in `restore` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Security ticket for the document service (CWE-22). Problem: the document store resolves names in four different ways and every entry point has its own hole: `put` strips `..` and still accepts absolute paths, `get` compares path prefixes (a sibling `store2` directory passes), `delete` never checks, and `rename` validates the source but not the new name. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Our static analysis flagged `Directory.register` (CWE-290): user names are only lower-cased and matched with `\w`, so `\uff41dmin` (full-width a), `\u0430dmin` (Cyrillic a), `\u017fupport` (long s) or `\u0441\u0435\u043e` (a Cyrillic `ceo`) get past the reserved-name list, a Cyrillic look-alike of an existing user such as `\u0455\u0441\u043e\u0440\u0435` for `scope` can be registered next to it, and the same e-mail address in another letter case opens a second account. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input. README.md defines the comparison rules (NFKC and case folding, single script, look-alike skeletons, e-mail normalisation); `confusables.py` holds the look-alike table.

Review comment on `AuthServer`: the authorization-code flow can be abused in several ways: redirect URIs are matched by prefix (`https://app.example.com/cb/../evil`, `.../cbx`), `state` is pasted into the redirect URL unencoded, codes can be redeemed twice and by other clients or for other redirect URIs, PKCE is ignored, confidential clients may omit their secret, the token request can ask for more scopes than the user granted (also on refresh), refresh tokens are neither rotated nor bound to a client, and expired access tokens still introspect as active. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload. README.md specifies the endpoints exactly (matching, encoding, binding, PKCE, scopes, rotation, revocation).

Security ticket for the edge proxy (CWE-444). Problem: `parse_request` is lenient in ways that let two parsers disagree about where a request ends (request smuggling): bare LF line ends, folded and `Name : value` header lines, repeated or malformed `Content-Length`, `Content-Length` together with `Transfer-Encoding`, `chunked, identity` and similar codings, `int()`-style chunk sizes (`0x5`, `+5`, `1_0`), trailers, control characters in values and targets, a missing or repeated `Host`. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests. README.md lists the exact grammar to accept; everything else must be a BadRequest, and valid requests (including pipelined ones) must parse unchanged.

Review comment on `is_valid_name`: `NAME` is `^(\w+\s?)*$`: a name such as `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!` makes the matcher try an exponential number of ways to split the word before it gives up, and a few such requests keep every worker busy (ReDoS). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

We had an incident review for the comment importer. Root cause: `strip_trailing` removes trailing whitespace with `re.sub(r"\s+$", ...)`. For a line that has a long run of spaces followed by a non-space character the regex engine retries the match from every position of the run, which takes quadratic time: a 50 KB comment keeps a worker busy for minutes. Close the hole in `strip_trailing` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

is_valid_email is unsafe: `EMAIL` nests a quantifier inside a quantifier (`([a-zA-Z0-9]+[._-]?)+`): a local part of 30 letters followed by a character that is not allowed makes the matcher try billions of combinations, so one malformed sign-up request can pin a CPU for minutes. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

A penetration test of the webhook settings reported a vulnerability: `HOSTNAME` is `^(([a-z0-9]+-?)+\.)+[a-z]{2,}$`: a label of 30 characters followed by something invalid makes the engine try every way to split the label into `[a-z0-9]+-?` pieces (exponential time), and the pattern also accepts labels ending in a hyphen (`a-.example.com`) and rejects the `xn--` labels of internationalised names. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Review comment on `is_amount`: `AMOUNT` wraps an alternation that can match the same digits in two ways inside a `+` (`(\d{1,3}(,\d{3})*|\d+)+`): a line of 30 digits followed by a letter takes exponential time to reject, and an attacker only has to upload a CSV with one such cell. The pattern also accepts `1234,567`, which is not a valid amount. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

A penetration test of the search indexer reported a vulnerability: `strip_tags` uses `<(.|\n)*?>`: for input with many `<` and no `>` (a text full of `<` characters) every `<` scans to the end of the document, with a slow alternation per character, and the indexer needs minutes for a 20 KB page. The pattern also treats `1 < 2 and 3 > 2` as a tag and deletes text. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Our static analysis flagged `auth_header` (CWE-798): the live gateway key `pgw_9f2c71ab33de4c0b8a17e5d6` is hard-coded in `payments.py`, and pasted into the README and `scripts/smoke.sh` as well; everybody with read access to the repository (and every fork, CI log and backup) holds a working production credential. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input. Remove it from every file in the repository (a rotated key will be issued separately). Importing the module must keep working without the variable being set.

load_settings is unsafe: the repository contains the production `.env` (database password, signing key and SMTP password) and has no `.gitignore`, so every clone has the secrets and the next `git add .` commits the next ones. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is. Keep the loader's behaviour: it must still read a local `.env` when one exists.

A penetration test of the reporting service reported a vulnerability: `config.ini` (committed) contains the database URL with its password (`postgres://app:S3cr3t-Pa55w0rd@db.internal:5432/shop`), so the production database password is in the repository and in every checkout that only needed the host name. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

A penetration test of the service startup log reported a vulnerability: the startup code logs the effective configuration with `log.info("config: %s", config)`; the dump contains the database URL with its password, API tokens and the signing key, and the log files are shipped to a third-party aggregator that every developer can search. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the pre-commit secret scanner. Root cause: the pre-commit scanner only knows AWS access keys that start with `AKIA`: private keys, GitHub and Slack tokens, temporary `ASIA` credentials and `password = "..."` literals sail through, which is how two leaked tokens reached the main branch last quarter. Close the hole in `scan_text` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

scan_text is unsafe: the scanner only matches known token formats and `password = ...` names: randomly generated credentials with other names or formats (`session_key = "q8Zk3VbN7xLp2WmTr9YdFh4JcAs6GeUo"`) are never reported, and there is no way to silence a reviewed false positive or to skip vendored files, so people disable the hook. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is. The existing rules and their output format must not change.

AuthService is unsafe: the account and reset flow has several weaknesses that add up to account takeover: passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-1 and any length is accepted, session ids are `md5(user + time)`, the reset endpoint tells attackers which e-mail addresses have accounts, the reset token is `md5(email + timestamp)` (predictable, stored in clear, never expires, reusable), the reset link takes its host from the `Host` header (so a forged header sends the victim's token to the attacker), resets do not end existing sessions, and nothing limits reset mails. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Review comment on `Shortener`: `create` fetches whatever URL a user submits (internal addresses, `file:` and `gopher:` URLs: SSRF) and stores `javascript:` URLs; short codes are sequential base-36 counters that anyone can enumerate; the preview page writes the fetched page title and the URL into HTML unescaped (stored XSS); and `delete` removes anybody's link. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

ExportService is unsafe: the order export writes customer-controlled text straight into CSV cells (formulas run when the finance team opens the file), lets customers export other customers' orders by passing their ids, has no limit on the number of rows, saves files under names taken from the request (`../../` escapes the export directory, links are followed), and builds the download headers from the same unchecked name. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Security ticket for the file sharing service (CWE-639). Problem: uploads are stored under the client's file name (`../` escapes the storage directory), file ids are a visible counter and `list_files` shows every user's files, anybody can mint a link for any file, the link signature is `sha256(secret + id + expires)` (extendable, not covering the download limit, compared with `==`) and expiry is never enforced, and the download counter is a read-modify-write on the shared store that two simultaneous downloads both pass. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

We had an incident review for the payment webhook endpoint. Root cause: the webhook endpoint authenticates with `sha256(secret + body)` compared by `==` and no timestamp (forgeable and replayable), credits every delivery of an event again (duplicate deliveries pay twice), trusts the amount and currency in the notification instead of the order, copies a `fields` object from the payload onto the order (so a forged event can set any attribute), crashes with a 500 on malformed bodies, and logs the whole payload including card data. Close the hole in `Billing.handle_webhook` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Security ticket for the web shop (CWE-1004). Problem: `session_cookie` sets the session cookie without `HttpOnly`, `Secure` or `SameSite`: any script injected into a page can read it (`document.cookie`), it travels over plain HTTP where it can be sniffed, and it accompanies cross-site requests. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

A penetration test of the dashboard reported a vulnerability: `logout` and `logout_all` only return a cookie-clearing header: the session stays alive in the server's store, so a copied cookie keeps working after the user logged out (and "log out everywhere" after a password change does nothing). Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the web shop login. Root cause: `login` authenticates the session id it was given and returns the same id: an attacker who plants a known session id in the victim's browser (a link with `?sid=...`, a cookie from a sibling sub-domain) is logged in as soon as the victim signs in (session fixation). Close the hole in `Site.login` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

We had an incident review for the dashboard sessions. Root cause: `user` never looks at the idle or absolute lifetime that `SessionStore` is configured with: a session created last month and last used last week still works, so a cookie left on a shared computer or leaked in a log is valid forever. Close the hole in `SessionStore.user` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Review comment on `find_user`: `find_user` builds its SQL by pasting the name into a string, so `' OR '1'='1` returns every customer and a name with an apostrophe (`O'Brien`) breaks the query. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `get_order` (CWE-89): `get_order` formats the order id straight into the statement with an f-string; ids arrive as strings from the URL, so `1 OR 1=1` returns every order and `0 UNION SELECT ...` reads other tables. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

search_products is unsafe: `search_products` concatenates the search term into a `LIKE '%...%'` pattern inside the SQL text (so quotes break out of the string), and `%`/`_` in the term act as wildcards instead of ordinary characters. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Review comment on `list_tasks`: `list_tasks` pastes the `sort_by` and `direction` query parameters into the ORDER BY clause; they cannot be bound as parameters, and an expression such as `(CASE WHEN (SELECT ...) THEN id ELSE -id END)` turns the ordering into a data-leaking oracle. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

We had an incident review for the bulk export. Root cause: `get_users` joins the ids it is given into an `IN (...)` list as text; ids come from a query string, so one element such as `2) OR (1=1` returns the whole table, and an empty list produces invalid SQL on some databases. Close the hole in `get_users` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Our static analysis flagged `export_table` (CWE-89): `export_table` and `column_names` insert the table name from the request into the statement; the name is only checked for being non-empty, so `sqlite_master`, `secrets` or `orders UNION SELECT ...` can be exported. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `posts_by_author` (CWE-89): user names are stored safely at registration, but `posts_by_author` later reads a name from the users table and pastes it into a new query; a user who registered as `x' OR '1'='1` makes the summary list everybody's posts (second-order injection). Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Security ticket for the blog engine (CWE-89). Problem: `add_comment` builds an INSERT with string formatting and runs it with `executescript`, which executes stacked statements: a comment such as `x'); DROP TABLE comments; --` destroys the table, and ordinary comments containing apostrophes fail. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Our static analysis flagged `search` (CWE-89): `search` builds its WHERE clause from the filter dict it receives: the *keys* (column names) are pasted into the SQL as well as the values, so a request with the key `1=1 OR city` (or a value containing quotes) changes the query. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

We had an incident review for the account service. Root cause: the account service has four injectable queries written in different styles: `login` pastes the credentials into the WHERE clause (`' OR 1=1 --` logs in as anyone), `search_accounts` concatenates a LIKE pattern, `audit_trail` takes `limit`/`offset` as text, and `purge` builds a DELETE with an f-string over a list of ids. Close the hole in `login/search_accounts/audit_trail/purge` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

A penetration test of the chat link previews reported a vulnerability: `link_title` accepts every URL that has a host part, so `file://localhost/etc/passwd`, `gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_INFO`, `dict://...` and `ftp://...` are handed to the fetcher and the server reads local files or talks to internal services for whoever posts a link. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

We had an incident review for the billing webhooks. Root cause: `is_allowed` only checks that the URL *starts with* the partner's address, so `https://hooks.partner.example.evil.io/`, `https://hooks.partner.example@evil.io/` and `https://hooks.partner.example:8443/` all pass and the service posts payloads wherever an attacker-controlled setting points it. Close the hole in `is_allowed` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Review comment on `is_trusted`: `is_trusted` compares the end of the host name with `str.endswith`, without a label boundary: `evilexample.com` and `notplaylists.partner.net` are "trusted", and anyone can register those, so the importer can be pointed at servers the allow-list was meant to exclude. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Security ticket for the avatar proxy (CWE-918). Problem: `fetch_avatar` blocks private targets by looking at the *text* of the host (`10.`, `127.`, `localhost`...); `http://2130706433/`, `http://0x7f000001/`, `http://127.1/`, `http://[::1]/`, `http://172.16.0.5/`, or a public-looking name whose DNS record points at `10.0.0.7` all reach internal services (SSRF). Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

We had an incident review for the outbound request policy. Root cause: `is_internal` only understands IPv4 (anything that is not an IPv4 address is reported as safe) and misses the shared 100.64.0.0/10 and multicast/reserved ranges, so `::1`, `fe80::1`, `fd00::1`, `::ffff:127.0.0.1` or a host name with an AAAA record into the private network pass the guard. Close the hole in `is_internal` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

A penetration test of the tenant allow-lists reported a vulnerability: `host_allowed` turns the tenant's wildcard pattern into an unanchored regular expression with unescaped dots, so `api.partner.net` also admits `api.partner.net.evil.io` and `apixpartner.net`, and `*.example.com` admits `evilexample.com`. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

A penetration test of the link unfurler reported a vulnerability: `unfurl` validates the URL the user typed but follows `Location` headers blindly, so a public page that answers `302 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` (or `//127.0.0.1/admin`, `file:///etc/passwd`) makes the server fetch internal resources: SSRF through redirects. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

A penetration test of the webhook sender reported a vulnerability: `send` checks the addresses a host name resolves to, and then hands the *host name* to the transport, which resolves it a second time. An attacker's DNS server answers the first lookup with a public address and the second with `10.0.0.5` or `169.254.169.254` (DNS rebinding), so the check passes and the request goes inside. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Review comment on `verify_token`: `verify_token` compares the secret with `==`, which stops at the first differing character; the response time reveals how long a correct prefix is, so a patient attacker can recover the token one character at a time. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Security ticket for the webhook receiver (CWE-208). Problem: `verify_signature` compares the expected HMAC with `==`: the comparison time depends on the number of matching leading characters, which lets an attacker forge a valid signature for a payload of their choice by guessing it character by character (and upper-case hex signatures from some senders are rejected). Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Review comment on `Auth.login`: `Auth.login` returns immediately for unknown user names and only runs the slow password hash for existing accounts, so response times reveal which names are valid (user enumeration through a timing side channel) and narrow down password-spraying targets. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Security ticket for the cookie signer (CWE-208). Problem: `safe_equals` is meant to be the constant-time comparison for cookie signatures, but it returns at the first differing character, so its running time leaks the length of the correct prefix: the signature of a forged cookie can be guessed one character at a time. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

We had an incident review for the nightly report job. Root cause: `save_report` checks `os.path.islink(path)` and opens the path afterwards; in the gap another user who can write to the shared directory replaces the file with a symlink to a file of the job's user (a credentials file, the crontab...) and the job overwrites that file: a classic time-of-check/time-of-use race. Close the hole in `save_report` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

We had an incident review for the upload handler. Root cause: `write_temp` names its file after the process id and checks `os.path.exists` before opening it: an attacker who can create names in the shared directory plants a dangling symlink at the predictable name (`exists` follows links, so the check passes) and the handler creates or overwrites a file of the attacker's choosing with upload data. Close the hole in `write_temp` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

Our static analysis flagged `save_secret` (CWE-276): `save_secret` creates the file with the default permissions (0666 minus umask, typically world-readable), writes the key, and only then calls `chmod 600`: between the write and the chmod any local user can open the file and keep the descriptor, and an existing file or symlink at the path is happily truncated or followed. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Review comment on `acquire_lock`: `acquire_lock` tests whether the lock file exists and creates it in a second step: two job instances started in the same instant both see no file, both create it and both run, which is exactly what the lock exists to prevent (the nightly run corrupted the ledger twice). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

A penetration test of the sign-up service reported a vulnerability: `register` asks the store whether the name exists and then inserts it, as two separate calls: two sign-ups for the same name that interleave both pass the check, both insert, and the second silently overwrites the first account's e-mail address, which hands the account (and its password resets) to the second requester. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Wallet.withdraw is unsafe: `withdraw` reads the balance, checks it, and writes the new value back as three separate store calls; two requests that interleave between the read and the write both see 100, both withdraw 80, and the account ends with 20 after 160 left it (double spend). The store has an atomic `add` for exactly this. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Review comment on `is_allowed_upload`: `is_allowed_upload` only looks at the text after the last dot: `shell.php.png` (executed as PHP by servers that honour any extension), `../../x.png`, `evil.png ` (trailing space dropped on Windows), names with NUL bytes (`x.php\x00.png`) and absurdly long names all pass the filter. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `accept_upload` (CWE-434): `accept_upload` believes the `Content-Type` header the client sent and never looks at the bytes: an HTML page with `Content-Type: image/png` and the name `avatar.png` is stored as an image, and served back to other users where browsers sniff it as HTML (stored XSS). Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Our static analysis flagged `store_upload` (CWE-73): `store_upload` writes the file under the name the client chose: `../../app/config.py` escapes the upload directory, `/etc/cron.d/x` goes wherever the process may write, and two users uploading `report.pdf` overwrite each other's file. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Security ticket for the file locker downloads (CWE-79). Problem: `download_headers` serves every stored upload inline with the content type the uploader declared: a user uploads `profile.html` (or an SVG) as `text/html`, shares the link, and the script runs in the application's origin (stored XSS); the file name goes unescaped into the header as well. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Review comment on `new_reset_token`: `new_reset_token` draws the token from Python's `random` module, a Mersenne Twister whose state can be recovered from a few hundred outputs; whoever can request resets for their own account can then predict the tokens issued to others. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

new_session_id is unsafe: `new_session_id` is the MD5 of the user name and the current time, so session ids of other users can be reconstructed by trying the few thousand timestamps around a known login (and two logins in the same instant collide), which is session hijacking. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Review comment on `new_otp`: `new_otp` uses the predictable `random` module, and formats the number without padding, so about one code in ten has fewer than six digits and users cannot enter it. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `generate_password` (CWE-338): `generate_password` uses the Mersenne Twister from `random`, and always puts one lowercase letter, one uppercase letter, one digit and one symbol in the first four positions, which both makes the password predictable from other outputs and removes entropy from the pattern. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

Security ticket for the developer portal (CWE-337). Problem: `new_api_key` re-seeds the global Mersenne Twister with `pid ^ time` before every key, so the whole key is determined by a seed with only a few thousand plausible values: anyone who knows roughly when a key was issued can regenerate it (and the re-seeding also makes every other user of `random` predictable). Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

pick_winner is unsafe: `pick_winner` turns one random byte into an index with `% len(entries)`: with more than 256 entries the later ones can never win, and with any list length that is not a divisor of 256 the first entries are favoured (modulo bias). The draw is only random in name. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.
render_comment is unsafe: `render_comment` inserts the author and the comment text into the HTML as they are, so a comment containing `

Security ticket for the link list (CWE-79). Problem: `render_link` writes the URL straight into the `href` attribute: a quote in the URL adds attributes (`" onmouseover="...`), and `javascript:` URLs (also in disguised forms such as `JaVaScRiPt:`, with tabs inside, or via character references) run script when clicked. Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

Review comment on `render_input`: `render_input` pastes the field name and its current value into double-quoted attributes; a value that contains a double quote closes the attribute and can add `onfocus`/`autofocus` handlers (reflected XSS when the form is redisplayed after a validation error). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Our static analysis flagged `render_config_script` (CWE-79): `render_config_script` embeds the app settings as JSON inside a `<script>` block; `json.dumps` does not escape `</script>`, so a setting value such as `</script><script>alert(1)</script>` (a user's display name, for instance) ends the block early and injects script. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

render_markup is unsafe: `render_markup` turns the wiki's light markup (`**bold**`, `_italic_`, `[label](url)`) into HTML by regex substitution on the raw text, so raw HTML typed into a page passes straight through, and `[x](javascript:alert(1))` becomes a script link. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

A penetration test of the notification templates reported a vulnerability: the template engine substitutes every `{{ value }}` into the page verbatim; only `{{{ value }}}` is supposed to be raw, but both forms skip escaping, so any template variable holding user text is an XSS hole. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Security ticket for the web framework (CWE-79). Problem: the error page template reflects the requested path (attacker-controlled) into several HTML contexts - the `<title>`, a `<meta content="...">` attribute and the body - without escaping, so a crafted link to a missing page runs script in the victim's browser (reflected XSS). Acceptance: hostile input can no longer do this, every documented behaviour still works, and the fix is in the code (not in the tests). Don't weaken the visible tests.

A penetration test of the community site reported a vulnerability: `render_profile` builds the member card from profile fields that members edit themselves: name and bio go into the page unescaped, `avatar` and `website` are written into `src`/`href` attributes without quoting or scheme checks (`x" onerror="...`, `javascript:` links). Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

extract_zip is unsafe: `extract_zip` joins every member name of an uploaded archive to the destination folder and writes it, so a member called `../../app/settings.py` (or an absolute path) is written outside the folder (zip-slip). fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

We had an incident review for the dataset importer. Root cause: `extract_tar` calls `TarFile.extractall` on uploaded archives as they are: members with `../` or absolute names, symbolic links that point outside the target and then get written through, and hard links to outside files are all honoured. Close the hole in `extract_tar` and anything that shares the flaw in this repository; normal users must notice nothing.

unbundle is unsafe: `unbundle` reads our own `BUNDLE1` container format and writes each entry to `dest/<entry name>` with no validation, so crafted entry names (`../..`, absolute paths) write anywhere the process can. fix it without breaking normal use, README.md says what normal is.

Our static analysis flagged `extract_zip` (CWE-22): the zip extractor tries to defend itself with `os.path.normpath(name).startswith('..')`, which lets absolute member names through (they replace the destination in `os.path.join`) and also wrongly rejects legitimate files whose names merely start with two dots, such as `..hidden.csv`. Harden the code. Existing behaviour for legitimate callers has to stay exactly as documented in README.md; there are tests for both the normal use and for hostile input.

A penetration test of the firmware update tool reported a vulnerability: `extract_zip` faithfully recreates symbolic links stored in an archive (unix mode in the zip entry) and its lexical `..` check passes for a later member like `evil/pwn.txt`; an archive can first plant `evil -> ..` (or an absolute link) and then write through it to anywhere. Fix it in the code so the whole class of problem is gone (not just the payload from the report) and keep everything legitimate working. README.md describes the intended behaviour.

Review comment on `extract_zip`: `extract_zip` reads every member completely into memory and writes it out, with no limit on the number of entries or on the uncompressed size, so a few kilobytes of zip can fill the disk and memory (zip bomb). Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Review comment on `install_plugin`: `install_plugin` trusts the `manifest.json` inside the uploaded package: the plugin `name` becomes a directory name (so `../../bin` escapes), and every path listed under `files` is joined to that directory unchecked. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Review comment on `unpack_all`: `unpack_all` recursively unpacks zip files found inside zip files without any limits, and joins member names to the destination unchecked: a deeply nested or wide archive exhausts the machine, and a nested archive can still write outside the destination. Please fix this properly and keep the existing functionality, including unusual but valid inputs. Nobody should be able to work around the fix with a variant of the payload.

Write `bigcalc.awk`: add and subtract arbitrarily long non-negative integers given as digit strings, one calculation per line, exactly. Read README.md. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions.

Write `qcsv2tsv.awk`: turn CSV records, including quoted fields with commas, doubled quotes and line breaks inside, into one TSV line per record. Read README.md. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions.

Write `rpn.awk`: evaluate one reverse-Polish expression per input line, with the stack words `dup`, `drop`, `swap` and precise error lines. Read README.md. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions.

Write `order.awk`: print a dependency order for `A B` lines (A before B), always taking the alphabetically smallest available name, and report cycles. Read README.md. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions.

Write `applydiff.awk PATCH ORIGINAL`: apply the hunks of a unified diff to a text file and print the result, or fail without output when a hunk does not match. Read README.md carefully. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions.

Write `route.awk`: answer shortest-route questions on an undirected weighted graph, choosing the route with the smallest place names when several are equally short. Read README.md carefully. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions.

Write `balance.awk`: read a plain-text ledger and print each account's balance exactly (no floating-point surprises like `-0.00`). Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `sessions.awk`: group page views into sessions per user (a pause of more than half an hour starts a new one) and print one line per session. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `latest.awk`: for each key (the first field) keep only the last line seen, but in the order the keys first appeared. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `histogram.awk`: a text histogram of numbers with a bucket width given on the command line as `w=10`. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `owners.awk`, which takes two files (pets and their owners, then visits with fees) and prints the total fee per owner. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `table.awk` to pretty-print a TAB-separated table from stdin: aligned columns, a dashed line under the header, numbers right-aligned. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `jobs.awk`: summarise a job log into one line per job with its outcome and duration. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `wrap.awk` which re-flows text to a given width (`w=NN`) and keeps paragraph breaks. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `top2.awk`: for each group print its two highest scoring entries with their rank. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `hourly.awk`: bucket timestamped readings by hour and print count and average per hour, including the empty hours in between. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

Write `kv.awk`: a small parser for configuration lines such as `host=db1; mode="a;b"; retries=3` that prints one tab-separated line per pair. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.

`stats.awk` should print count, minimum, maximum and average per endpoint, but its output order is random, the average is truncated and the header line pollutes the numbers. Fix it. Plain POSIX awk only (the tests run `awk -f`, which is mawk here): no gawk extensions such as `asort`, `gensub` or `strftime`.
Write `snapshot.sh SRC DEST STAMP`: archive a directory as `DEST/backup-STAMP.tar` with a predictable layout.
Write `restore.sh [-f] ARCHIVE DEST [PATH...]`: extract a snapshot, optionally only some paths, without clobbering existing files unless forced.
Write `mirror.sh SRC DEST`: bring DEST in line with SRC the way a minimal rsync would, reporting what it copied and removed.
Write `rotate-snaps.sh DEST KEEP`: keep the newest KEEP snapshot directories and delete the older ones.
Write `hardlink-snap.sh SRC DEST STAMP`: make a new full snapshot directory in which unchanged files are hard links to the previous snapshot's files.
Write `verify.sh ARCHIVE SRC`: check a snapshot tar (as made by `snapshot.sh`) against the live directory and report the differences.
Write `snapshot-x.sh SRC DEST STAMP EXCLUDES`: like the tar snapshot, but skipping files that match patterns from a file.
Write `latest.sh [--list] DEST`: name the newest backup archive in a directory, or list all, with a same-day run counter in the names.
`backup.sh` makes a tar of a directory, but it loses hidden files, falls apart on names with spaces and happily continues when something fails. Fix it.
Write `prune-old.sh DEST DAYS TODAY`: delete backup archives older than DAYS days relative to a given date, but always keep the newest one.
`tidy.sh` is supposed to turn every `.txt` file in the folder into `.md`, and it works until somebody has a file with a space or a dash in its name. Fix it so it handles any file name.

Write `tidy.sh` so that it lowercases the extension of every file in the current directory (`IMG_01.JPG` becomes `IMG_01.jpg`). Details, including what to do when the lowercase name is already taken, are in the README.
Our scanner names files `scan 3.pdf`, `scan 10.pdf`, `scan 118.pdf` and they sort badly. Write `tidy.sh` that pads the first number in every file name to four digits, as described in the README.
Add the last-modified date (UTC, `YYYY-MM-DD_`) in front of every file in a folder, but don't do it twice to files that already carry such a prefix. Please write `tidy.sh` per the README.
I have a messy tree of subfolders and want every file moved into a single `flat/` folder. Name clashes must not lose data; write `tidy.sh` as the README describes.
Music files are named `Artist - Title (Year).ext` and I want `Year - Artist - Title.ext` instead. Write `tidy.sh`; the README lists the exact pattern and what to do with files that do not fit it.
Some of the files we receive have names that break our build tools. Write `tidy.sh` that rewrites them to a safe alphabet; the rules and the tie-breaking for clashes are in the README.
Write `tidy.sh` to give extension-less files a proper extension by looking at their first bytes (png, gif, pdf, zip, jpg, shell scripts). The README lists the signatures.

Write `rn.sh`, a small batch-prefix tool with a dry-run mode and an undo. The README spells out the interface, the log format and the error cases.

Write `remap.sh MAPPING.csv`: it applies a list of renames from a CSV file, including swaps and cycles, quoted names and moves into new folders. The README has the exact format and the reporting rules.
Write `greet.sh`, a tiny CLI that greets someone: `-n NAME`, `-c COUNT`, `-u`. The README lists the exact output and what counts as a usage error.
Write `convert.sh -f UNIT -t UNIT VALUE...` which converts lengths between metres, kilometres, miles, feet and inches. Exact format and error handling are in the README.
Write `lines.sh [-n N] [-s] [-r] [FILE...]`: take the first N lines, skip blank ones, reverse the result; reads stdin when no file is given. README has the order of operations.
Write `tagname.sh` that turns version strings into tag names: optional prefix and suffix, optional removal of a leading `v`, optional lower-casing. README has the order of the steps.
Write `envcheck.sh`, a pre-flight check that verifies required environment variables are set and non-empty, and can print `export` lines for the good ones. The README has the exact rules.
Write `retry.sh [-n TRIES] [-d SECONDS] [-q] COMMAND [ARG...]`, a wrapper that re-runs a flaky command. README describes the messages, exit status and argument handling.
Write `cols.sh [-d DELIM] [-H] SPEC` which prints selected columns of delimited text from stdin; with `-H` the first line holds column names that SPEC can use. The README defines SPEC.

Write `cfg.sh`: an argument parser that understands both short and GNU-style long options (including `--name=value`, bundled short flags and `--`) and prints the parsed configuration. The README lists the options and the output lines.
`sendmsg.sh` mishandles its options: the options leak into the message body, it chokes on bodies with spaces, and unknown options are silently ignored. Fix the argument handling.
Write `chores.sh`, a tiny chore-list manager with subcommands (`add`, `list`, `rm`), a global `-f FILE` and `-v`, and per-subcommand options. README has the file format and every message.
Write `human.sh [-b 1000|1024] [-p N]`: read byte counts from stdin and print them as `1.5 KiB`-style strings. The README gives the unit names, rounding and the treatment of bad lines.
Write `csv-cols.sh FILE COL...`: keep chosen columns of a CSV file (by header name or position), with proper quoting.
Write `csv-sum.sh FILE COL`: the exact sum of a numeric column, two decimals.
